title: Which voice speaks to you
hookLine: each reader finds one Bhagat who feels like a friend

cards: Which of these voices would you sit next to on a long bus ride? Not which one is greatest. The Granth doesn't rank them, and neither will i.
Just which one you'd want beside you. The one who asks plainly for flour and a cow. The one who dreams of a city with no sorrow in it.
The one who says hard things with a grin. Some readers find, after a while, one voice they keep going back to.

teach.h: DHANNA ASKS FOR FLOUR AND A COW.
teach.b: Listen to how differently they speak.

Dhanna, the farmer, in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 695, makes an arti, a hymn of worship, that reads in paraphrase like a shopping list handed to God: flour, lentils, a little ghee, shoes, good clothes, a cow, a horse.
A man asking his Lord for what a household needs, without embarrassment.

teach.h: RAVIDAS DREAMS OF A CITY WITHOUT SORROW.
teach.b: Ravidas, in Raag Gauri on Ang 345, describes Begampura, the place without sorrow: no tax, no fear, no one second or third class. That city, he says, is his home.
Kabir, in his saloks, is the friend who tells you the truth to your face and doesn't soften it, often with a picture from the loom or the market.

teach.h: KABIR AND FARID: SHARP TONGUE, LONG ACHE.
teach.b: And Farid, in Raag Asa on Ang 488, sings of hearts dyed in love for God, verses that ache for the Beloved. A farmer's frankness. A dream of a fair city.
A sharp tongue. A long ache. All in one book, all sung as gurbani, none placed above another.
So the question isn't which one is right.

teach.h: NONE RANKED; WHICH ONE CAN YOU HEAR?
teach.b: It's which one you can hear. Someone in a hard month might lean toward Farid. Someone tired of a world that sorts people might lean toward Ravidas.
Someone who prays best in plain words might lean toward Dhanna. Gurbani speaks of the Lord as a friend, mit or sajan. A favorite Bhagat doesn't replace that.
It's more like a friend who shows the way to the Friend.

how: Sikhs read and sing the Bhagats' hymns as part of the Guru, and some readers return again and again to particular shabads, including Bhagats' hymns, that they hold dear.

o: a friend; the Lord as the Friend
a teacher who must be obeyed
a stranger met on the road

p: asks plainly for flour and a cow
says hard things to your face

s: the Granth ranks the Bhagats from greatest to least
they're all in the same book, sung as gurbani, and none is placed above another.
Dhanna's arti asks God for everyday things like flour and ghee
a farmer asking for what a household needs, on Ang 695.
Begampura is a city without sorrow in Ravidas's hymn
he describes it in Raag Gauri and calls it his home.

games.q: a friend asks which Bhagat is the best one to read. what's the answer today's lesson gives?
o: the one whose voice you can hear; the Granth ranks none of them.
games.why: the question isn't which one is right but which one you can hear; the Granth doesn't rank them.

practice: Let the four voices pass by, one at a time: Dhanna's plain list, Ravidas's city, Kabir's sharp line, Farid's ache.

Don't choose too fast; just notice which one you'd want to hear again tomorrow, and if none stands out, that's an answer too, and the week of reading will help. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Mit. Gurbani's word for a friend: the Lord as a friend, and a favorite Bhagat as a friend who shows the way to the Friend.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a friend; gurbani calls the Lord a friend.

carryVoice: Your line: a friend in the granth. No ranking, just a voice you can hear. Seven hundred ninety-nine days, and counting.
